feedback: When magnesium burning is sorted as combustion, confirm it AND prompt: it also gains oxygen to form magnesium oxide, so it is oxidation too — the categories are not mutually exclusive.

If a reaction is sorted only by surface appearance, redirect to the defining evidence: is a fuel burning? is oxygen being gained? is ONE substance splitting on heating? is one element replacing another?
For copper carbonate -> copper oxide + carbon dioxide, name why it is thermal decomposition: heat breaks one compound into simpler substances (watch for the released gas and colour change).
activities.intendedInsight: Each reaction family has a tell-tale observable signature, and you classify by reasoning from that evidence rather than by memorising definitions in isolation; some reactions legitimately belong to more than one family.
learnerActions: Take a shuffled set of reactions, some presented as word equations (e.g. copper carbonate -> copper oxide + carbon dioxide) and some as one-line observed scenes (e.g. a strip of magnesium flares white and leaves a powder; a piece of iron dipped in blue copper sulfate becomes coated with pink-brown metal).
Sort each reaction into one of four families: combustion, oxidation, thermal decomposition, displacement.
For each card, state the evidence that justifies your choice: heat and light, a gained oxide, one substance splitting apart on heating, or one element swapping for another.
Flag any reaction that seems to belong in two families and explain why (e.g. magnesium burning).
activities.title: Name that reaction: sort by evidence

feedback: If a learner expects burning magnesium to lose mass, track the oxygen: magnesium + oxygen -> magnesium oxide, so the solid oxide is HEAVIER because oxygen from the air was added — while total mass (metal + oxygen) is unchanged.
For a reaction where the solid appears to lose mass (e.g. wood burning), point out the lost mass has left as gases — total mass is still conserved once the escaping gases are counted.
If the atom check is skipped, prompt the learner to list the elements on each side before deciding the equation is complete.
activities.intendedInsight: Reactions rearrange atoms rather than create or destroy matter, so total mass is conserved even when the weighable solid appears to change; word equations and the atom check make this explicit for every reaction type.
learnerActions: Complete word equations with missing reactants or products, e.g. methane + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water, and copper carbonate -> copper oxide + carbon dioxide.

After writing each equation, check that every element present before the reaction also appears after it. A word equation shows which elements are present, not how many atoms of each, so this check is consistent with atoms being neither created nor destroyed but does not prove it on its own.

Draw or compare before/after mass bars and explain that the TOTAL mass stays the same because atoms are only rearranged; then note that the solid you can actually weigh may appear to gain mass (magnesium takes in oxygen from the air) or lose mass (wood releases gases) depending on whether gas is absorbed or given off.
Match each reaction to its tell-tale sign: heat+light, gains oxygen, one substance splits into two or more simpler substances on heating, an element swapped out.
activities.title: Complete the word equation and check conservation

feedback: When the carbonate is heated, point to the limewater turning cloudy as the signature that carbon dioxide was released — evidence of thermal decomposition.
For the displacement station, highlight the deposited metal and solution colour change, and connect it to the more reactive element replacing the less reactive one.

If a learner misreads heating a carbonate as melting, contrast melting (same substance, reversible) with decomposition (new substances form, here a gas is released, and often there is a colour change, e.g. green copper carbonate turning to black copper oxide).
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing each reaction type and its signature (flame, oxide layer, gas released on heating, deposited metal) is intended to build perceptual hooks that later classification can draw on.
learnerActions: Visit four stations that each trigger one reaction type: light a fuel (combustion, heat and light), heat a metal in oxygen (oxidation, an oxide forms), heat a carbonate so the released gas turns limewater cloudy (thermal decomposition, CO2 detected), and dip a metal into a solution of a salt of a less reactive metal, e.g. iron into copper sulfate (displacement, a metal deposits with a colour change).
Watch each reaction auto-produce its word equation and note the observable signature.
Switch to a 'name that reaction' mode where the label is hidden and classify each reaction from its evidence alone.
activities.title: Reaction bench: observe the signatures before sorting

feedback: If the learner predicts the powder weighs less, revisit: metal + oxygen -> metal oxide means oxygen is added, so the solid mass INCREASES while total mass is unchanged.
If oxidation is thought to mean only rusting, group burning, rusting, and magnesium-burning together: all are gaining oxygen, with rusting the slow case and burning the fast case.
For the wood comparison, note the escaping gases carry away the 'lost' mass — total mass is still conserved once gases are counted.
activities.intendedInsight: Combustion of magnesium is oxidation: the metal combines with oxygen from the air, so the solid product gains mass. Burning does not destroy matter; where mass seems to be lost (wood, candle) it has escaped as gases, so total matter is conserved.
learnerActions: Before burning, weigh a coil of magnesium ribbon and predict whether the mass of the white powder afterwards will be more, less, or the same — and state WHY.

Heat the ribbon in a crucible with a lid, lifting the lid slightly now and then to let air in while keeping the white smoke in. Then weigh the crucible, lid and product and compare with the crucible, lid and ribbon before heating.
Compare your prediction with the result and explain what combustion/oxidation actually did to the magnesium.
Reconcile this with wood burning, which leaves only light ash: where did the wood's mass go?
activities.title: Predict–Observe–Explain: weighing burning magnesium

feedback: If a learner treats all burning as producing only CO2 and water, point to soot and carbon monoxide as evidence of incomplete combustion when oxygen is limited.
Reinforce that both complete and incomplete combustion are still combustion — the fuel burns in oxygen — they differ in how much oxygen is available and therefore in the products.
activities.intendedInsight: Combustion is not a single outcome: the amount of available oxygen changes the products, distinguishing clean complete combustion from sooty incomplete combustion.
learnerActions: Compare complete combustion of a hydrocarbon fuel such as methane or candle wax (products carbon dioxide and water) with its incomplete combustion (products including carbon monoxide and soot).
Identify, from described evidence such as soot deposits or a smoky yellow flame, whether combustion was complete or incomplete.
Explain why limited oxygen leads to incomplete combustion and the formation of soot and carbon monoxide.
activities.title: Complete vs incomplete combustion
